title: Adaptive quarantine and tokenized capacity reservations for node upgrades
creator: Anika Patel
description:
Problem: During planned upgrades and node retirements in Dedicated fleets we observe small but measurable regressions in 99th percentile latency and transient throughput drops when we drain hosts aggressively. Current drain logic is time-based and binary (node drained vs active) and doesn't account for tail-latency SLOs or per-customer throughput guarantees.

Goal: Implement an adaptive quarantine + tokenized capacity reservation mechanism that allows us to retire/upgrade nodes while preserving committed throughput contracts and percentile latency SLOs. The system should: 1) allocate lightweight 'capacity tokens' representing throughput/slot reservations that follow customer workload during drain operations; 2) pace KV-cache eviction and request migration based on live latency signals; 3) provide ops controls to prefer capacity-preserving slow drains or aggressive drains for emergency maintenance; and 4) expose metrics and tracing for post-mortem and runbook automation.
acceptance_criteria: Capacity token abstraction implemented in runtime router and Dedicated control plane; tokens are created per-drain and can be attached/detached to customer routes.
Drains can be configured in two modes: conservative (latency-preserving) and expedited (time-bounded) with clear SLO/regression tradeoffs visible in console.
E2E tests show <5% added 99th percentile latency variance across simulated retirements for production-like workloads when conservative drains are used.
Observability: new dashboards for token allocations, live reserved units, and drain pacing signals available in Redwood Console; alerts for token exhaustion.
Runbook updated and an automated rollback trigger exists when histograms exceed configured thresholds during a drain.
Documentation: design doc and operator guide published, plus a migration plan for existing fleets to opt into tokenized drains.
Security review completed for token lifecycle and control-plane APIs (KMS usage confirmed).
implementation_steps: Design: final design doc in Confluence with sequence diagrams and API contracts.
Control plane: add token issuance/lease API and persistent token registry scoped to Dedicated pools.
Router/runtime: wire token checks into request routing and KV cache eviction so requests using a token preferentially stay on target capacity until token TTL/usage is consumed.
Drain pacing: implement PID-ish controller that uses tail-latency and queue-depth signals to modulate migration rate and cache eviction rate.
Ops UI: add console controls to create drains, pick mode, and view live token state and SLO metrics.
E2E and chaos tests: inject host retirements in staging with synthetic traffic patterns and validate metrics/alerts.
Rollout: staggered rollout starting with non-critical pools, collect metrics for 2 weeks, then enable for higher tiers.
Post-deploy: iterate on tuning knobs based on observed workload shapes and update autoscaling/placement heuristics accordingly.
progress_updates: 2025-02-12: Kickoff meeting. Identified primary SLO tradeoffs and stakeholders (SRE, runtime, console, PM).
2025-02-18: Design draft uploaded: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/DF/ENG-98123+Adaptive+Quarantine. Feedback from SRE: prefer token TTLs over hard reservations to avoid deadlocks.
2025-02-24: Prototype control-plane token registry merged to feature branch (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/2287). Basic token lifecycle wiring added.

2025-02-27: Runtime patch for token-aware routing landed in staging branch; initial microbenchmarks show token attach adds 0.3% p99 CPU overhead but prevents 40-60% of request migrations during drains.

2025-03-01: Integration tests failing intermittently: observed a race when tokens expired mid-request causing 502s. Reproduced locally; mitigation strategy drafted to extend TTL during in-flight requests.
2025-03-03: TTL-extension fix implemented and new test added. Requesting design review and SRE signoff before enabling conservative mode on pilot pool.
Blocked: pending a small kube-drain behavior change from infra team (see dependency ENG-34211) to allow graceful pod termination hints.
decisions: Use tokenized soft-reservations instead of hard preemption leases to reduce risk of starving other customers.
Conservative drain mode will prioritize 99th percentile latency preservation; expedited mode will be time-limited and can be forced by on-call for emergencies.
Token TTLs will be extended for in-flight requests to avoid mid-request token expiration; TTL extension policy documented in design doc.
Tokens are scoped at the route/customer level and billed as metadata only; no extra monetary charge for customers under current pricing model.
risks: Token exhaustion leading to inability to place new requests if reservations are accidentally leaked; mitigated by TTLs and periodic reconciliation job.
Increased control-plane state and complexity; may increase outage blast radius if registry becomes unavailable — added leader election and fallback to current drain behavior.
Race conditions causing mid-flight request failures during TTL changes; tests added but edge cases remain under investigation.
Potential unforeseen cost increase on Dedicated fleets if conservative drains force more nodes to remain warm; will monitor with billing dashboards and add autoscale policy hooks.
